newsitem.title: UK: Options-Cocoa vols rise as futures rally.
newsitem.headline: Options-Cocoa vols rise as futures rally.

text.p: Cocoa volatilities soared this week, stirred by the explosive futures rally, while those for coffee stayed strong although values seemed to have peaked.
Cocoa options saw fairly brisk activity after a prolonged lull as futures values gained by nearly 10 percent earlier this week on a spate of speculative short-covering.
"With the (futures) market rally, the volatilities have increased," said one market maker.
There was a lot of interest around July 1,100 stg and 1,200 stg calls as players turned bullish.

"The volatilities have gone from trading around 21-22 percent to 26-27 percent," he said. "People are much more friendly towards the market and are willing to look at options as an upside protection against shorts."
Cocoa futures, emerging from a nine-month downtrend last week, rallied sharply on Monday and Tuesday, with May chalking up gains of 81 stg gains.
But the rally appeared to have stalled and the market stepped back slightly since then as it tried to consolidate the gains.

Thursday's easier sentiment may have reflected high arrivals from Ivory Coast, contradicting comments by Ivorian Commodities Miniser Guy-Alain Gauze who said earlier this week that the total 1996/97 cocoa crop would be less than one million tonnes.
In coffee, volatilities stayed firm this week.
May at-the-money strikes saw volatilities at 47 percent and July at 48 percent on Wednesday against 48-49 percent last week.
May $1,700-July $1,750 call spread was traded at a discount of two percent earlier in the week. On Thursday, July premium widened to four percent.

"People were expecting vols to come off this week but they continue to stabilise with May trading at 46-47 percent at-the-money calls and July trading at 49 percent in the last couple of days," said one options trader.
July is traditionally at a premium to May as people take protection against frost risk in Brazil. The last severe frosts in 1994 sent coffee prices to $4,000.
"I don't think July will go below 45 percent. Even that is risky. July usually holds high premium all the year round," he said.
Traders said coffee vols were not expected to fall sharply unless futures values tumble by hefty $100-$200.
May robusta futures propelled to a new nine-month-high of $1,825 a tonne on Tuesday, erasing last week's peak of $1,820.
But the market continued its roller-coaster ride and prices have since retreated to trade at a low of $1,672 on Thursday. -- Jalil Hamid, London newsroom +44 171 542 4985
